attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter post, stated in his voice.

semantics.note: The source says 'there is not', which the draft turns into 'won't be'. That shift is acceptable given the forward-looking 'unless... very soon'. The proposition keeps 'likely' on cheaper, but the condition text lists cheaper as required, which overstates it. 'AI compute' is a reasonable target given the data-centre context.

contract.note: The contract correctly says the claim cannot be scored. 'Enough demand', 'very different', 'very big way' and 'very soon' have no stated threshold, capacity or deadline. Any test would require boundaries the speaker never supplied.

evidence.note: October 2026 analyst piece from Sculptor. It frames whether demand can absorb planned capacity as an open question. It is an analyst framework, not an observed outcome, so it is context only.

reviews.rationale: The conditional has no measurable demand threshold, no defined technological exception and no usable deadline ('very soon'). The packet contains only analyst context. Without adding criteria the speaker never stated, the claim cannot be scored.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his own post.

semantics.note: The normalised text keeps all components: the $1.1T in commitments, the dependence on growth, customer protests and the market's valuation verdict. It is a present-tense observation.

contract.note: The plain reading is ordinary. It treats the figure as outstanding nominal commitments, reads 'contingent' as economic dependence and sets the period to June 2026. The ambiguities about valuation scope and accounting basis are fairly flagged.

evidence.note: Microsoft's October 2025 call confirms one $250B OpenAI Azure commitment. That is one contract from an earlier date, not the combined June 2026 total.
June 2026 report of Anthropic reversing an unpopular billing change after developer anger. It partly bears on the customer-protest component but cannot settle the compound claim.
OpenAI's March 2026 private round at $852B post-money. Its date and transaction type differ from a June market verdict on an IPO valuation.

reviews.rationale: Nothing in the packet reconciles a combined $1.1T commitment total for June 2026. Dependence on growth and the market's valuation verdict are not established, and the key IPO reporting could not be read. Customer resistance has only partial contemporaneous support. The evidence neither supports nor contradicts the compound claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion. The Doctorow paraphrase that follows is separate and is not part of this claim.

semantics.note: The draft faithfully keeps the compound claim: billions in losses, plus subsidised accounts that allow about $8,000 a month of tokens for $200.

contract.note: Reading the claim as 'some accounts allow' about $8,000 at API prices is fair and ordinary. The contract rightly separates an API-price discount from a below-cost subsidy, and its loss period (2025) is reasonable.

evidence.note: Anthropic's S-1 (available Oct 26) reports a $42.0B net loss for 2025. That is still billions after removing $34.3B of fair-value changes, so it supports the loss component only. It is a company filing.
SemiAnalysis says subscriptions are more generous than about $2,000 a month, but the readable text shows no $8,000 figure, token counts or costs.
June 2026 report confirms Max 20x costs $200 a month. It does not establish the token value or Anthropic's serving cost.

reviews.rationale: The loss component holds: the S-1 shows multi-billion 2025 losses even excluding fair-value changes. The $8,000-for-$200 figure and the subsidy are not established, because the readable test shows no number and there is no cost evidence. Nothing contradicts either part. Because the specific usage claim is unsettled, the compound claim as a whole is unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words, followed by his supporting revenue-share argument.

semantics.note: 'May as well not have' is a hyperbolic idiom, not a probability hedge. The draft correctly reads it as asserting that Microsoft's non-OpenAI AI business is insignificant, and it keeps the 'outside of OpenAI' qualifier.

contract.note: The plain reading is fair and matches the context: exclude OpenAI as a paying customer and assess the commercial significance of the rest. Using paid adoption without converting it to revenue is an ordinary test. The Q3 FY26 period is the latest reported before the post.

evidence.note: Microsoft's Q3 FY26 earnings call (quarter ended March 31, published April 29) reports over 20M paid M365 Copilot seats. That is substantial paid AI adoption beyond OpenAI's Azure purchases. It is a company disclosure.

reviews.rationale: The contract's contradiction condition is met. Microsoft disclosed over 20M paid Copilot seats in the target quarter, which is substantial paid adoption separate from OpenAI's compute purchases. Even on a hyperbolic reading, that is not an AI business Microsoft 'may as well not have'. The evidence is a company disclosure, but it is an audited-context earnings statement that the contract accepts as a source.
